proposals.name: Explicit research question or puzzle framing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract poses an explicit question, puzzle, or apparent contradiction in the field that the paper then resolves (e.g., phrasing like 'why do X happen' or 'would it be more effective to...'). Score 0 if the abstract simply states 'we propose method X for task Y' with no question or puzzle framing at all, just a direct method announcement.
proposals.rationale: R23 explicitly frames the puzzle of why prior works found negative attention heads before resolving it, and R43 poses the direct research question 'would it be more effective to separate highly conflicting objectives...'; both are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model rewards this framing while the scorecard does not.

proposals.name: Mechanistic root-cause explanation of a phenomenon
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract identifies a specific causal mechanism explaining WHY an observed problem or effect occurs (not just that it occurs), e.g. 'LN makes tokens similar in magnitude because it normalizes within each token'. Score 0 if the abstract only describes symptoms or lists components/results without ever explaining the underlying cause.
proposals.rationale: R07 explains the causal mechanism behind Layer Normalization's failure mode, and R23 explains the mechanism behind copy suppression that resolves earlier confusion about negative heads; both dense_high_card_low, versus purely descriptive component lists in dense_low_card_high rows like R01 and R12.

proposals.name: Specific engagement with named prior work vs. generic reference
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract names a specific prior paper, model, or method and states precisely how this work extends, refutes, or settles an open question raised by it. Score 0 if the abstract only refers vaguely to 'existing methods', 'prior work', or 'other algorithms' with no specific work named or engaged.
proposals.rationale: R42 explicitly states it 'significantly extend[s] \citet{arvind2024hierarchy} and settle[s] their open questions' (dense_high_card_low), while R05 and R01 only reference 'other high performing uncertainty based active learning algorithms' and 'existing long-tail learning methods' generically (both dense_low_card_high).

proposals.name: Quantitative attribution of effect to the proposed mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reports a quantitative decomposition of how much of an effect or variance is explained/attributed to the specific proposed component (e.g., 'explains 76.9% of the impact', 'RMSE of 1.24%', 'correlation r=0.94'). Score 0 if the abstract reports only an aggregate task-performance number with no attribution or decomposition analysis.
proposals.rationale: R23 quantifies that its mechanism 'explains 76.9% of the impact' and R56 reports precise reconstruction RMSE and correlation figures; both dense_high_card_low, in contrast to dense_low_card_high rows like R40 and R44 that report only headline aggregate percentage gains.

proposals.name: Acronym-stacking for sub-components
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract coins three or more new acronyms for the method and its internal sub-components (e.g., a method acronym containing further acronymed sub-modules), making the contribution read as assembled parts. Score 10 if the abstract uses plain descriptive language with at most one new named method/acronym.
proposals.rationale: R01 stacks IKL containing IUR and ICL, and R10 introduces FHBI with no plain-language alternative offered; both dense_low_card_high, versus the single, plainly-described contributions in dense_high_card_low rows like R23 and R42.

proposals.name: Unstructured laundry-list of properties vs. single coherent claim
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract ends with an unstructured list of desirable properties strung together (e.g., 'high accuracy, rapid convergence, robustness..., strong generalization') that are asserted rather than shown to follow from one insight. Score 10 if the abstract centers on one coherent claim or insight that all reported evidence directly supports.
proposals.rationale: R12 closes with a disconnected list of properties (accuracy, convergence, robustness, generalization) and R18 bundles several loosely related sub-contributions (classifier, visualization method, augmentation technique, attention mechanism) without a unifying thread; both dense_low_card_high, versus the single unifying finding organizing R23 and R47 (dense_high_card_low).

proposals.name: Contextualized vs. decontextualized improvement magnitude
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if reported improvement numbers are given with clear baseline context and a magnitude that is credible and well-anchored (e.g., percentage points with named baseline, or explained-variance figures). Score 0 if the abstract leads with a very large relative percentage (e.g., '384% faster', '1822% reduced memory', '53% increase') without stating the absolute baseline or why such a large gain is plausible.
proposals.rationale: R40 foregrounds '384% faster sampling' and '1822% reduced memory consumption' and R44 highlights a '53% increase over selected baselines' with no absolute context; both dense_low_card_high, versus the precisely anchored figures in R23 and R56 (dense_high_card_low).

proposals.name: Comparison against a strong external reference point
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract benchmarks the method against a real external reference point outside the paper's own ablation suite, such as human expert performance, a named competition win, or an established leaderboard/psychometric correlation. Score 0 if the abstract only compares against other automated baselines drawn from the same benchmark suite as the paper itself.
proposals.rationale: R27 compares its system's word error rate directly against professional human lipreaders, and R47 reports its method 'constituted one of the winning entries to the Open Graph Benchmark Large Scale Challenge at KDD Cup 2021'; both dense_high_card_low, versus purely intra-suite baseline comparisons typical of dense_low_card_high rows like R01 and R34.

proposals.name: Concretely scaled resource-building effort
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract specifies concrete scale and composition of a newly built dataset or benchmark, with named numbers and content types (e.g., '340M images with human pose, depth, and surface normal annotations', '3,886 hours of video'). Score 0 if the abstract mentions building a dataset/benchmark/environment suite without any concrete scale or composition numbers.
proposals.rationale: R19 specifies its HumanVerse dataset as '340M images with comprehensive annotations' and R27 specifies '3,886 hours of video'; both dense_high_card_low, versus R37's HIVEX which names five environments but gives no size/scale figures for the benchmark itself (dense_low... actually card-favored side, showing the scorecard is insensitive to this absence).

proposals.name: Explicit trade-off reasoning behind a design choice
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly names a tension between two competing goals and explains the reasoning behind how the proposed method balances or resolves it. Score 0 if the abstract simply asserts the method 'achieves both X and Y' or 'improves both A and B' without ever discussing why these goals are normally in tension.
proposals.rationale: R33 reasons explicitly about the catastrophic-forgetting tension when injecting multiple kinds of knowledge, and R26 reasons about the trade-off between personalization fidelity and text editability; both dense_high_card_low, versus R41's unreasoned dual claim of 'enhanced attack capability' and 'significantly accelerates generation' (dense_low_card_high).

proposals.name: Generic superlative density as unsupported filler
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract uses words like 'novel', 'significant(ly)', or 'state-of-the-art' three or more times as unsupported boosting adjectives rather than to introduce a specific, evidenced claim. Score 10 if such claims of novelty or significance are used sparingly and each instance is immediately tied to a specific fact, mechanism, or number.
proposals.rationale: R01 repeats 'novel'/'significantly improve'/'state-of-the-art' as recurring boosters with little specific tie-in, and R05 similarly stacks 'state-of-the-art', 'consistently outperforms', and 'high performing' as generic praise; both dense_low_card_high, versus the sparing, evidence-tied claims in R23 and R42 (dense_high_card_low).

proposals.name: Articulated task difficulty vs. benchmark-name checklist
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explains WHY the chosen evaluation setting is difficult, informative, or non-redundant (e.g., explaining that six benchmarks are highly correlated and thus redundant, motivating a sparse subset). Score 0 if the abstract's evaluation justification consists only of listing standard dataset names (e.g., 'CIFAR10, CIFAR100, Tiny ImageNet') with no explanation of why they constitute a meaningful test.
proposals.rationale: R56 explains that benchmark scores are redundant due to high correlation and that this motivates a sparse, information-dense subset, and R43 explains why finding a common descent direction becomes hard as the number of conflicting objectives grows; both dense_high_card_low, versus the bare dataset-name checklists in R05 and R34 (dense_low_card_high).

proposals.name: Named concrete real-world deployment setting
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract situates the method in a specific, named real-world deployment context (e.g., a named spacecraft/rover, a named clinical or industrial pipeline). Score 0 if the abstract only asserts generic 'real-world applicability' or invokes 'real-world problems' in the abstract without naming any concrete deployment setting.
proposals.rationale: R21 names the Curiosity rover operating on Mars as the deployment context, and R20 names the cryo-EM structural biology and drug discovery pipeline; both dense_high_card_low, versus R37's HIVEX which invokes 'real-world problems' and 'ecological challenges' only abstractly without naming a concrete deployment (dense_low_card_high).

proposals.name: Surprising/emergent finding reported as discovery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reports an unexpected or surprising empirical finding uncovered during the work, beyond the intended headline result (e.g., 'a vision-only model not pretrained with text-image alignment surprisingly outperforms CLIP'). Score 0 if the abstract reports only the expected, intended outcome (method X beats baseline Y on the target metric) with no discovery-flavored or surprising finding.
proposals.rationale: R48 reports the surprising finding that DINO, despite lacking text-image pretraining, outperforms CLIP on fine-grained tasks, and R35 highlights that 'pure data scaling makes a strong 3D perception capability' emerge without specialized 3D architecture; both dense_high_card_low, versus the purely-expected performance wins reported in R01 and R16 (dense_low_card_high).

proposals.name: Rhetorical register proportionate to technical scope
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract uses dramatically inflated rhetorical framing disproportionate to a narrow technical contribution (e.g., calling the work 'a whistleblower for the community', or labeling an incremental technique 'the breakthrough'). Score 10 if the abstract's rhetorical register is measured and proportionate to the actual scope of the technical contribution, even when the claimed result is large.
proposals.rationale: R15 frames itself as acting 'as a whistleblower for the community' and R03 refers to its own technique as 'the breakthrough'; both dense_low_card_high, versus the measured, precise language used even for large claims in R23 and R42 (dense_high_card_low).

proposals.name: Mechanistic account of why the method works
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the abstract offers a causal explanation for the method's effect, not merely a report that it works. 10 = the abstract names a specific mechanism and states how it produces the improvement, in terms a reader could argue with (e.g. 'masking past tokens prevents over-attending to recent tokens'; 'gates operating in flat regions correspond to better generalization'; 'normalizing within each token makes tokens similar in magnitude, so positional context is lost'). 5 = a mechanism is gestured at with one clause but not connected to the observed effect. 0 = purely operational description ('we propose X, which consists of modules A, B, C, and achieves state-of-the-art') with no account of why X should help. Do not reward the mere presence of the words 'we hypothesize' or 'insight' if no mechanism follows.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R08 both spend a third of the abstract on the causal story (recency over-attention; flat-region gates) and are dense-high/card-low (0.753/0.102 and 0.841/0.318). R33 diagnoses exactly what LayerNorm does to token magnitudes before proposing DTN (0.595/0.089). By contrast R56 (0.071/0.673) lists NODE-SAT's three modules and four virtues with no mechanism, and R07 (0.156/0.824) names IUR/ICL without saying why exploiting adjacent-epoch uncertainty should reduce head bias. A checklist bank can score 'method described clearly' and 'novelty claimed' on all four, which is plausibly the missed dimension.

proposals.name: Specific falsifiable diagnosis of prior methods' failure
proposals.instruction: Score how concretely the abstract identifies what goes wrong with existing approaches, as opposed to asserting that they are limited. 10 = a named, checkable failure mode with the condition under which it bites (e.g. 'methods converge on a shortcut that uses only the most recent turn's image, so retrieval fails when the modification references history'; 'refined Gaussian conditional and hyperprior distributions mismatch, increasing rate cost in cross-domain tasks'). 5 = a real but generic limitation ('prior methods are expensive', 'require many negatives'). 0 = boilerplate gap language ('remains underexplored', 'existing methods have limitations', 'theoretical understanding is incomplete') with no diagnosis. Judge only the sharpness of the stated failure, not whether the fix is convincing.
proposals.rationale: R23 (0.781/0.282) and R40 (0.683/0.108) are both dense-high while the scorecard rates them mid-low; each opens with a precise, testable claim about how the prior method breaks. R01 (0.664/0.128) similarly states that pitch alone cannot cover paralinguistics and that feature choice requires hand-engineering. Compare R36 (0.150/0.782) and R22 (0.031/0.906), which name no failure at all and simply report beating seven baselines — a bank rewarding 'motivation present' and 'baselines compared' would over-credit them.

proposals.name: Contribution removes a requirement rather than adding machinery
proposals.instruction: Score whether the paper's advance consists of eliminating something the field currently believes is necessary (a component, a supervision source, an architectural change, a hand-engineering step, a training phase) while retaining or improving performance. 10 = an explicit requirement is dropped and the abstract says performance is maintained or improved without it (e.g. 'no negative examples and only simple augmentations'; 'virtually no architectural changes and no auxiliary classifiers or decision networks'; 'eliminates manual feature selection'). 5 = simplification is claimed but nothing specific is removed. 0 = the method is strictly additive — a new module, loss, or stage bolted onto an existing pipeline. Purely additive work can still be good work; score only the subtractive property.
proposals.rationale: The dense-high side is full of subtraction: R04 (0.814/0.254) removes negatives and complex augmentations, R25 (0.753/0.215) removes intermediate classifiers and architectural change, R01 (0.664/0.128) removes hand-engineered paralinguistic features. The dense-low/card-high side is dominated by addition: R19 (0.010/0.912) adds an auto-regressive iteration to AdvGAN, R07 (0.156/0.824) adds two modules to existing long-tail methods, R55 (0.088/0.853) adds a diffusion model on top of demonstration selection. A criterion bank counting components, novelty claims and benchmark wins will systematically reward the additive side.

proposals.name: Counter-expectation finding about an actionable community belief
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract reports a result that contradicts a belief the field currently acts on, stated plainly as a finding. 10 = a clearly stated reversal or surprise about a default practice or default architecture, with the surprising direction named (e.g. 'the vision-only model DINO, not trained with text-image alignment, surpasses CLIP on fine-grained perception'; 'pure data scaling yields strong 3D perception with no 3D-specific architecture or objective'; 'shallow CLIP layers, not deep ones, help grounding'). 5 = a mild or expected-direction finding presented as surprising. 0 = every reported result confirms what the method was designed to show. Judge the belief's reach: a reversal about a widely used default scores higher than a reversal about a niche hyperparameter setting.
proposals.rationale: R14 (0.732/0.061) and R15 (0.856/0.262) are the two clearest reversals in the slice and both sit far above their scorecard rank; R30 (0.787/0.292) likewise reports that six benchmarks collapse onto one common factor. The contrast that makes the criterion sharp is R43 (0.003/0.880), which also says 'contrary to previous findings' but about the bootstrap rate of random forests — the scorecard's highest-scoring reversal and the dense model's lowest-ranked abstract in the whole slice, which suggests a bank crediting contrarian framing without weighting the reach of the belief being overturned.

proposals.name: Explains prior puzzling results or settles named open questions
proposals.instruction: Score whether the work retroactively accounts for observations other researchers have already reported but could not explain, or resolves a question explicitly posed in prior literature. 10 = the abstract states what previously reported phenomenon its result explains, or names the prior work whose open question it closes, with a quantitative handle where possible (e.g. 'this explains why multiple prior works studying narrow tasks found negative heads that favored the wrong answer'; 'our results extend [prior] and settle their open questions'; 'explains the high correlations within and between benchmark scores'). 5 = connects to prior findings only by claiming consistency with them. 0 = the abstract's results stand alone; nothing outside the paper becomes more understandable.
proposals.rationale: R49 (0.853/0.301) is the purest case — copy suppression is offered as the explanation of a documented anomaly — and R46 (0.894/0.294) explicitly settles two cited open questions; both are dense-high with mid scorecard ranks. R30 (0.787/0.292) explains a known correlation structure. Nothing on the dense-low/card-high side does this: R37 (0.169/0.811) and R22 (0.031/0.906) report their own numbers only. Explanatory debt-repayment is exactly the kind of value a fixed criterion bank is unlikely to have an item for.

proposals.name: Claim calibration: superlatives and vague margins penalized
proposals.instruction: Score how well the strength of language matches the evidence described. 10 = claims are bounded and specific, with the comparison class named and the scope of the claim limited to what was tested ('improves R-D performance compared with other latent refinement counterparts'; 'early training results on data gathered by the Curiosity rover'; 'all models face challenges, especially for complex prompts'). 3 = unbounded superlatives whose comparison class is left vague or hedged ('consistently outperforms all other high performing algorithms'; 'outperforms baselines by notable margins'; 'a 53% increase over selected baselines'). 0 = self-aggrandizing framing of the contribution itself ('the breakthrough is...', 'our research acts as a whistleblower'). Penalize inflation independently of whether the underlying result might be true.
proposals.rationale: R35 (0.073/0.816), R38 (0.102/0.641), R17 (0.046/0.701) and R22 (0.031/0.906) all sit high on the scorecard while the dense model puts them in the bottom decile; each carries an unbounded or hedge-qualified superlative. Meanwhile R32 (0.635/0.078) explicitly labels its results 'early' and R16 (0.864/0.243) reports that every model it tested struggles, and both are dense-high with near-bottom card scores. A bank with an item like 'states a clear performance claim' would score confident inflation as a strength.

proposals.name: Interpretable, denominator-transparent magnitude reporting
proposals.instruction: Score whether the numbers in the abstract can be interpreted by a reader without access to the paper. 10 = quantities on a scale the reader can situate, with baseline and unit stated (e.g. 'SuperGLUE zero-shot from 55.7 to 59.2'; 'word error rate of 40.9% versus 86.4% for professional lipreaders'; 'reconstructs each benchmark score with 1.24% RMSE'). 5 = relative multipliers with a clearly named comparator but no absolute level ('2-10x memory reduction versus prior methods'). 0 = percentages or ratios whose denominator or comparator is unstated or implausible on its face ('1822% reduced memory consumption', '384% faster', 'improves performance by half over selected baselines'), or no quantity at all where one is clearly available. Score the interpretability of the reporting, not the size of the gain.
proposals.rationale: R18 (0.249/0.791) and R17 (0.046/0.701) both score in the scorecard's top quartile while the dense model rejects them, and both report percentage gains whose denominators are unstated and whose magnitudes are hard to read. R56 (0.071/0.673) reports no numbers at all yet claims accuracy, convergence, robustness and generalization. On the dense-high side R52 (0.692/0.194), R06 (0.753/0.102) and R30 (0.787/0.292) report situated absolute levels. A bank item for 'quantitative results reported' cannot distinguish these.

proposals.name: Comparison anchored to an external human or expert standard
proposals.instruction: Score whether performance is placed against a reference outside the paper's own baseline set — human performance, expert judgment, a professional practice, or a documented deployed system. 10 = an external human/expert standard is measured or used as the evaluation instrument on the same data (e.g. 'professional lipreaders achieve 86.4% or 92.9% WER on the same dataset'; 'evaluation conducted with 11 scientists across correctness, relevance, and scientific accuracy'). 5 = a strong published external system is used as the anchor but no human standard. 0 = only self-selected algorithmic baselines, or an unnamed 'state-of-the-art'. Anchoring must be on comparable data to score above 5.
proposals.rationale: R52 (0.692/0.194) and R16 (0.864/0.243) both carry human anchors and both are dense-high with bottom-quartile scorecard ranks; R29 (0.725/0.052) reports agreement against human-to-human agreement and has the second-lowest card score in the slice. The dense-low/card-high rows anchor only to algorithmic baselines: R36 (0.150/0.782), R41 (0.177/0.801), R60 (0.073/0.794). An external standard makes the number mean something, and it is easy for a bank to omit.

proposals.name: One controlling idea versus enumerated contribution list
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract is organized around a single idea that generates its parts, or is a list of separable deliverables. 10 = one claim from which the components follow, so a reader can restate the paper in a sentence. 4 = several components introduced with distinct acronyms, each defended separately, but a discernible unifying claim. 0 = a numbered or serial list of independent contributions with no organizing claim ('a classifier is presented; a visualization adaptation is proposed; a novel augmentation is introduced; window sizes are evaluated; an attention mechanism is also proposed'), or a chain of 'we establish / we reveal / we prove / we propose / we devise / we test'. Judge structure, not length; multi-component methods are fine if one idea licenses the components.
proposals.rationale: R03 (0.005/0.655) and R26 (0.136/0.826) are both serial contribution lists that the scorecard likes and the dense model puts near the floor; R21 (0.194/0.922) has the slice's highest card score and stacks a backronym, a theorem extension and a speedup. Against these, R06 (0.753/0.102), R25 (0.753/0.215) and R33 (0.595/0.089) each reduce to one sentence. A bank that counts distinct contributions will reward exactly the wrong side of this contrast.

proposals.name: Consequence scope: what others can now do
proposals.instruction: Score the reach of what becomes possible if the paper's claim holds. 10 = the result unblocks work for people who are not working on this method — a new regime becomes reachable, a field-scale resource is created, or a capability class opens (e.g. scaling to graphs with hundreds of millions of nodes and winning an open large-scale challenge; a foundation model serving many downstream cryo-EM/cryo-ET tasks without fine-tuning; a 340M-image annotated corpus; a benchmark that compresses six benchmarks to under 3% of their size). 5 = a real improvement confined to the method's own subfield. 0 = a parameter-level or setting-level result whose consequence is a better default for one algorithm, or a theoretical bound under assumptions narrow enough that no practice changes. Judge the reference class of the problem, not the size of the reported delta.
proposals.rationale: R04 (0.814/0.254), R59 (0.818/0.326), R24 (0.897/0.163) and R30 (0.787/0.292) are dense-high with mid-to-low card scores and all change what other groups can attempt. The dense-low/card-high side concentrates narrow-consequence work with strong rubric surfaces: R43 (0.003/0.880) tunes the bootstrap rate of random forests across 36 datasets with a significance test, R44 (0.195/0.749) bounds momentum's generalization error under strong convexity, R53 (0.118/0.765) connects pruning to differential privacy with two datasets. All three would score well on rigor items while the dense model ranks them in the bottom quintile.

proposals.name: Evidence covers the regime where the claim should break
proposals.instruction: Score whether the reported evaluation includes the hardest or most adversarial setting for the paper's own claim, rather than the setting most favorable to it. 10 = the abstract names a stress regime chosen because it strains the claim — uncurated or in-the-wild data, extreme scale, cross-domain transfer, multiple languages, or a held-out condition the method was not designed for. 5 = several standard benchmarks in one domain. 0 = a single benchmark suite, or benchmarks that match the method's design assumptions exactly, with breadth claimed via dataset count alone. A large count of similar datasets does not raise the score; a single well-chosen breaking-point test does.
proposals.rationale: R57 (0.676/0.151) evaluates on uncurated Instagram video rather than only curated Kinetics, R04 (0.814/0.254) pushes to hundreds of millions of nodes, R16 (0.864/0.243) spans four input languages including Farsi, R12 (0.864/0.228) adds probing beyond the six task datasets — all dense-high, all card-low. Meanwhile R26 (0.136/0.826) tests on CIFAR-10/100 only and R22 (0.031/0.906) on one benchmark suite, both near the top of the scorecard. This suggests the bank counts datasets rather than asking whether any of them could have falsified the claim.

proposals.name: States a limitation, cost, or scope boundary honestly
proposals.instruction: Score whether the abstract volunteers something that cuts against its own case. 10 = a concrete cost, failure, or boundary is stated in the same register as the claims ('9-16% overhead in computation'; 'at marginal loss of prediction accuracy'; 'early training results'; 'all models face challenges, especially for more complex prompts'). 5 = a limitation is mentioned but framed as future work. 0 = the abstract contains no cost, no boundary and no unfavorable result; every sentence is favorable. Score the presence and specificity of the self-imposed constraint, not its severity.
proposals.rationale: R16 (0.864/0.243) and R32 (0.635/0.078) both volunteer unfavorable information and both are dense-high with near-floor card scores; R25 (0.753/0.215) concedes accuracy loss in the same sentence as the speedup. Uniformly favorable abstracts cluster on the other side: R56 (0.071/0.673), R36 (0.150/0.782), R41 (0.177/0.801). A criterion bank built from 'does it state contributions clearly' will treat unmixed positivity as strength.

proposals.name: Borrowed framework is load-bearing, not decorative
proposals.instruction: Score whether an imported theory, biological analogy, or piece of machinery from another field is doing real work. 10 = the import resolves a specific technical obstacle the paper names, or pays back a result in the source field (e.g. Gumbel-Softmax invoked because learning toward discrete gate values is otherwise not backpropagatable; compressed sensing for orthogonal polynomials that also yields improved sample-complexity bounds for learning decision trees). 5 = the import is used, and its role is stated, but any comparable tool would serve. 0 = the analogy supplies vocabulary and motivation only ('biologically plausible', 'inspired by neural circuit dynamics', 'drawing upon insights from robotics') while the actual method could be described without it. Ignore how fashionable the borrowed framework is.
proposals.rationale: R08 (0.841/0.318) and R54 (0.590/0.048) both import external machinery to clear a named obstacle and both give something back, and both are dense-high with low card scores. R17 (0.046/0.701) devotes most of its abstract to why ring attractors are biologically plausible and then reports only an aggregate Atari gain; R55 (0.088/0.853) marries subgoal learning from robotics with diffusion models for demonstration ordering. Both rank high on the scorecard, which likely credits interdisciplinary novelty framing without asking whether the framing is removable.

proposals.name: Contribution not self-reducible to an existing technique
proposals.instruction: Score whether, by the abstract's own description, the contribution survives reduction to something already known. 10 = the abstract introduces an object or claim with no existing equivalent, and any equivalence it notes is a proof obligation it discharges rather than a deflation of its novelty. 4 = the contribution is a recombination of two known methods, presented as new. 0 = the abstract itself states the equivalence that deflates it (e.g. the method is 'effectively equivalent to applying goal data augmentation to SL methods', which prior work already did; the sampler 'maintains mathematical equivalence to conventional sampling strategies' and differs only in speed) while still framing the work as a novel method. Judge the reducibility, not whether reduction makes the work useless.
proposals.rationale: R09 (0.123/0.797) concedes its method is equivalent to goal data augmentation and then contrasts itself with work that applied goal data augmentation; R18 (0.249/0.791) states mathematical equivalence to standard sampling, making the contribution an implementation speedup dressed as a sampling method. Both sit in the scorecard's top quartile and the dense model's bottom quartile. Against them, R58 (0.814/0.287) introduces model parameters that are natural-language strings, which has no reduction, and is dense-high/card-mid. A novelty item in a bank scores the word 'novel'; this criterion scores whether the abstract undercuts it.

proposals.name: Reproducibility detail is substantive, not a boilerplate promise
proposals.instruction: Score the informativeness of the resource and reproducibility content. 10 = the abstract supplies specifics that let a reader size the work before reading it — corpus scale and annotation types, item counts, model counts, protocol (e.g. '3,886 hours of video'; '340M images with pose, depth and surface normal annotations'; 'n > 5000 LLMs, d = 28,632 items'; models and output modes enumerated by name). 5 = a real released artifact is named or linked, with modest detail. 0 = a promise contingent on the outcome ('code will be made publicly available upon acceptance', 'open-sourced upon publication'), a broken or placeholder link, or a bare URL with no accompanying description of what is in it. Do not award points for the mere existence of a link.
proposals.rationale: R52 (0.692/0.194), R24 (0.897/0.163) and R30 (0.787/0.292) are dense-high with low card scores and give sizing detail rather than promises. The other direction is striking: R07 (0.156/0.824), R02 (0.231/0.845) and R55 (0.088/0.853) all defer code to acceptance or publication, and R43 (0.003/0.880) links to a literal '<placeholder>' — yet all four are in the scorecard's top quartile, with R43 near its ceiling. That pattern is the clearest sign in the slice of a bank item rewarding artifact-availability language regardless of whether anything is actually available or described.

proposals.name: Failure-mode diagnosis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a precise prior failure, explains when or why it occurs, and targets it directly; score 0 when motivation is generic and no concrete failure mode is specified.
proposals.rationale: R01 precisely identifies catastrophic forgetting under multiple knowledge injections, while R22 identifies the historical-turn shortcut in multi-turn retrieval. By contrast, R46 mainly asserts robustness and generalization without diagnosing a specific failure.

proposals.name: Mechanism-to-problem fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when each major design choice has a clear causal role in fixing the diagnosed problem; score 0 when the method is mainly a list of modules with no explanation of why they should help.
proposals.rationale: R06 connects soft policies to improved training gradients, and R48 derives distribution regularization from a specific probability-mismatch mechanism. R45 names multiple components but gives little causal account of how they jointly resolve long-tail errors.

proposals.name: Unifying design principle
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when one coherent principle explains the architecture, training procedure, and observed benefits across settings; score 0 when the contributions are disconnected add-ons or independently motivated tricks.
proposals.rationale: R08 uses rank restriction as a single explanation for both personalization and retained editability, while R55 unifies appearance, depth, normals, and geometry. This coherence is less evident in module-heavy abstracts such as R46.

proposals.name: Explanatory discovery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work reveals a non-obvious mechanism or relationship that explains behavior and yields testable implications beyond a performance gain; score 0 when it only proposes a method and reports aggregate results.
proposals.rationale: R19 explains copy suppression, calibration, and self-repair with intervention-based evidence, and R07 derives a quantitative expressivity hierarchy for spectral GNNs. R02 primarily enumerates architectural additions and benchmark improvements without a comparable explanatory discovery.

proposals.name: Causal contribution isolation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when ablations, interventions, probes, or controlled comparisons isolate which component causes which effect; score 0 when only the complete system is compared against baselines.
proposals.rationale: R19 quantifies the impact of a particular head and separates mechanisms of self-repair, while R44 identifies the separate necessity of continuous relaxation and iterative refinement. R03 claims extensive experiments but does not isolate the contributions of RSFT and RVA.

proposals.name: Failure-aligned stress testing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation deliberately contains the difficult cases implied by the problem statement and uses metrics that expose the claimed failure; score 0 when evaluation is limited to generic or easy benchmarks unrelated to the stated challenge.
proposals.rationale: R22 constructs demands tied to historical turns, and R29 tests combinations of spatial, numeric, and attribute reasoning in scientific images. These evaluations are more diagnostically aligned than the broad benchmark claims in R33.

proposals.name: Transfer under meaningful shift
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract demonstrates transfer across genuinely different tasks, domains, objects, architectures, or distribution shifts, preferably without retraining; score 0 when evidence comes from one narrowly matched setting.
proposals.rationale: R13 reports downstream cryo-EM and cryo-ET use without fine-tuning, R28 evaluates newly encountered objects, and R54 transfers from web video pretraining to multiple downstream tasks. This distinguishes real generalization from single-dataset success.

proposals.name: Compositional constraint handling
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method preserves and satisfies several interacting requirements simultaneously, with evidence on their combinations; score 0 when it handles isolated attributes or a single constraint only.
proposals.rationale: R18 combines 2D context, 3D grounding, visual prompts, and varied formats, while R44 supports style-related clustering without losing topic structure. R22 likewise requires current edits to retain historical information, exposing compositional ability.

proposals.name: Quality-resource Pareto evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract quantifies resource savings together with maintained or improved quality under a meaningful matched comparison; score 0 when efficiency is merely asserted or quality and cost are reported separately.
proposals.rationale: R14 reports orders-of-magnitude faster inference while outperforming DDPM, and R24 reports large memory reductions while scaling to massive graphs. R57 similarly states a memory reduction alongside a measured computation overhead, making the tradeoff auditable.

proposals.name: Diagnostic benchmark validity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the dataset or benchmark is designed to remove leakage and uninformative samples, cover meaningful difficulty axes, and distinguish competing capabilities; score 0 when it is merely a collection of tasks with no validity argument.
proposals.rationale: R11 explicitly filters uninformative samples and answer leakage, R29 separates spatial, numeric, and attribute comprehension with human evaluation, and R59 defines public data with explicit synthesis and detection tasks. These are stronger evaluation contributions than simply listing environments or datasets.

proposals.name: Theory-to-method coupling
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a theorem or derivation directly determines a design choice or prediction that is empirically tested; score 0 when theory is detached from the algorithm or appears only as an after-the-fact bound.
proposals.rationale: R48 derives its regularizer from a stated distributional mismatch, R16 turns an objective equivalence into Q-conditioned supervised learning, and R60 uses smoothing and influence analysis to construct its unified model. R26 provides bounds but does not clearly connect them to a new intervention.

proposals.name: Quantitative claim calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when claims include exact effect sizes, denominators, baselines, settings, and relevant resource or uncertainty information; score 0 when the abstract relies on vague superiority language, isolated records, or unspecified comparisons.
proposals.rationale: R20 gives results over 36 datasets with explicit bootstrap ranges and prediction accuracies, and R18 reports exact AP improvements on named benchmarks. In contrast, R33 says performance improves by half without clearly specifying the comparison scope, while R46 says only that most datasets improve.

proposals.name: Boundary and sensitivity disclosure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract states important limitations, failure cases, sensitivities, or conditions under which conclusions change; score 0 when it presents only unqualified positive claims.
proposals.rationale: R05 reports strong random-seed sensitivity in GNN evaluation, and R29 acknowledges that all evaluated models struggle with complex prompts. Such boundary information is absent from broad claims like those in R03, which emphasizes vulnerability without clearly delimiting attack conditions.

proposals.name: Operational reproducibility detail
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract specifies data sources, task protocol, model scale, comparison procedure, and usable artifacts sufficiently to audit or reconstruct the contribution; score 0 when implementation and evaluation details are opaque.
proposals.rationale: R15 specifies judge scales, training data contents, bias controls, model sizes, and throughput, while R59 describes recording modalities, benchmark tasks, metrics, and public artifacts. These details make the claims more auditable than the generic description in R31.

proposals.name: Open-question closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work explicitly tests a prevailing assumption or resolves a named theoretical or empirical open question and states the resulting implication; score 0 when novelty consists only of renaming or recombining familiar components.
proposals.rationale: R07 directly settles open questions about spectral GNN expressivity, R05 challenges the homophily assumption and proposes a broader perspective, and R38 overturns expectations about text-aligned vision encoders by finding DINO competitive. These conceptual closures go beyond routine architectural variation.

proposals.name: Mechanistic Causal Account
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives a specific, plausible mechanism linking the intervention to the claimed improvement and reports evidence consistent with that mechanism; score 0 when it only names components and asserts better performance.
proposals.rationale: The dense model appears responsive to explanatory depth in R02 and R37, whereas many scorecard-favored papers such as R22 and R39 state formal ideas without clearly connecting them to observed behavior.

proposals.name: Bottleneck-to-Design Alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the paper identifies a concrete failure mode or bottleneck and each central design choice directly addresses it; score 0 when the method is presented as a generic collection of modules unrelated to a diagnosed problem.
proposals.rationale: R01, R25, and R47 tightly connect diagnosed shortcomings to targeted designs, while R49 and R51 mainly list architectures and claimed benefits without an equally sharp problem-to-design chain.

proposals.name: Nontrivial Conceptual Advance
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work introduces a genuinely new way to formulate, understand, or solve the problem that would generalize beyond the named implementation; score 0 when the contribution is primarily a routine module, tuning change, or renamed combination.
proposals.rationale: Dense-high examples R02, R06, and R37 offer new conceptual lenses, while scorecard-high examples R08, R34, and R49 emphasize incremental architectural changes and broad performance claims.

proposals.name: Theory Predicting Observations
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when theoretical analysis yields a concrete prediction, bound, or explanation that is directly tested and meaningfully informs the algorithm; score 0 when theory is detached background or consists only of generic guarantees.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R48 use analysis to explain specific model behavior, whereas R43 and R39 foreground theory but provide little abstract-level evidence that it predicts the reported empirical results.

proposals.name: Component-Level Attribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract indicates controlled ablations, comparisons, or analyses that isolate the contribution of each important component; score 0 when all components are introduced together and only aggregate performance is reported.
proposals.rationale: R31 explicitly reports that continuous relaxation and refinement are each crucial, and R44 investigates alternative optimization recipes; R05 and R49 rely more on undifferentiated claims of superiority.

proposals.name: Diagnostic Evaluation Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation is designed to distinguish the claimed capability from shortcuts, leakage, or easy cases, with task-specific measures; score 0 when evaluation is merely a list of standard benchmarks and one headline metric.
proposals.rationale: R03 removes uninformative and leaked samples, and R47 constructs a dataset exposing historical-turn shortcuts; in contrast, R08 and R49 primarily present standard benchmark results.

proposals.name: Distribution-Shift Evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract tests clearly specified unseen domains, tasks, populations, or conditions and shows what transfers; score 0 when it only claims generalization or evaluates familiar in-distribution benchmarks.
proposals.rationale: R10 evaluates newly encountered objects, R16 adapts without source-data access, and R41 tests both heterophilic and non-heterophilic settings; vague generalization language in R49 and R51 receives less credit.

proposals.name: Efficiency-Capability Tradeoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method delivers a quantified resource gain while preserving or improving the target capability, making the tradeoff explicit; score 0 when efficiency is merely claimed, unmeasured, or purchased by sacrificing the main objective.
proposals.rationale: R26, R53, and R58 quantify speed or memory gains alongside quality, while R05 and R28 make impressive speed claims without equally clear characterization of the full capability-cost tradeoff.

proposals.name: Relevant-Regime Scaling Evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract demonstrates performance, stability, or feasibility at a scale that is materially relevant to the stated problem and explains what enables it; score 0 when 'large-scale' is asserted without scale-specific evidence.
proposals.rationale: R07, R42, and R58 tie their claims to unusually large datasets, graphs, or downstream workloads; scorecard-favored R54 and R55 invoke broad practical scope with less evidence of operation at the claimed regime.

proposals.name: Reproducible Operational Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract specifies data sources, task protocol, model changes, comparison setting, and measurable outcomes sufficiently to reconstruct the experiment; score 0 when the proposal is mainly aspirational or omits the operational details needed to interpret its claims.
proposals.rationale: R07, R18, and R48 provide concrete datasets, protocols, changes, and numerical effects, whereas R40, R51, and R54 leave important experimental particulars abstract despite strong claims.

proposals.name: Fair Comparative Calibration
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when comparisons identify strong and appropriate baselines, use comparable conditions, quantify margins, and avoid overstating what the evidence supports; score 0 when 'state of the art' is unsupported or comparisons are ambiguous.
proposals.rationale: R13 and R35 provide explicit comparative margins and task settings, while R04, R39, and R49 use broad superiority language with limited abstract-level detail about baseline fairness.

proposals.name: Compositional Capability Gain
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when combining the method's components or skills enables a qualitatively new, compositional capability demonstrated across interacting inputs or tasks; score 0 when components operate independently and only improve isolated scores.
proposals.rationale: R06, R19, R47, and R50 describe structured combinations that support abstraction, knowledge composition, multi-turn reasoning, or tool use; R08 and R34 mainly report isolated classification improvements.

proposals.name: Honest Scope Boundaries
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract clearly states limitations, difficult cases, tradeoffs, or conditions under which the method may fail while calibrating its claims; score 0 when it presents universal-sounding success with no boundary conditions.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R30 explicitly identify benchmark weaknesses and model failure cases, while R05, R39, and R51 make expansive claims with little discussion of limitations.

proposals.name: Data-Centric Problem Insight
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work reveals how data quality, structure, labeling, or sampling governs the task and turns that insight into a principled intervention; score 0 when data are treated as interchangeable inputs or a dataset is introduced without a substantive insight.
proposals.rationale: R03, R41, and R60 expose redundancy, graph structure, or evaluation sensitivity as central issues; scorecard-favored dataset papers such as R52 and R54 emphasize availability and breadth more than a demonstrated data principle.

proposals.name: Mechanism-Focused Stress Testing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when experiments deliberately perturb, ablate, or vary the conditions relevant to the proposed mechanism and reveal when the method succeeds or fails; score 0 when evaluation reports only aggregate wins on fixed test sets.
proposals.rationale: R30 varies reasoning dimensions and languages, R41 examines split sensitivity and graph homophily, and R37 uses ablation to study self-repair; R04 and R51 provide far less abstract-level evidence of mechanism-focused stress tests.
